name: game market intelligence tools
title: Best Game Market Intelligence Tools in 2026
summary_line: Data services that estimate competitor revenue, downloads, wishlists and genre trends so studios can size a game before and after launch.
definition: Game market intelligence tools collect and model public store data, panel data and publisher feeds to estimate how other games perform. They report downloads, revenue, owners, wishlists, live events and audience mix by title, genre or region. Studios use them to judge a pitch, pick a genre, benchmark a launch and set realistic sales targets.
intro: Before a studio commits a year of development, someone asks what comparable games earned. The tools below try to answer that, but they answer different versions of it: mobile store revenue, Steam owners, wishlists and sales forecasts, live-event calendars, or regional market reports for Asia. We compared ten services by reading each vendor's homepage, about page and, where reachable, pricing page, and we weighed what a small or mid-size studio can get without an enterprise contract. We did not buy subscriptions or check any estimate against a real revenue report, so every figure the tools produce should be treated as a model. Three planned vendors, Newzoo, SteamDB and Streams Charts, could not be opened during our check and are not ranked; SteamSpy and Niko Partners were added after we read their pages.

criteria.heading: Which storefront the numbers come from
criteria.text: Steam, mobile stores and consoles each need different data sources. A tool that is strong on Apple and Google store data says little about a Steam launch, and the reverse holds too. Identify where your next game will be sold, then check which store or platform each vendor actually covers. Console data is rarer and often limited to a few titles, so look for it named in the vendor's own pages rather than assuming it is there.

criteria.heading: Estimate quality and how it is explained
criteria.text: Every service here estimates; none sees real accounting. The useful ones say what they measure, how large the error might be, and what distorts results. Some print a margin of error beside each figure. Others rely on panel data or store APIs and state that in a sentence. Treat vendors that give a single clean number with no method note carefully, and cross-check two sources before betting a budget on one.

criteria.heading: Data you can act on, not only browse
criteria.text: A studio needs wishlist trends, comparable-game revenue, live-event calendars and audience overlap, not a leaderboard. Check whether you can export data, reach it by API or ask questions through an assistant. Two vendors on this page advertise MCP or API access. Also look at depth per game: a few headline numbers are less useful than dozens of data points per title that you can filter by genre or tag.

criteria.heading: Access model and price visibility
criteria.text: None of the ten tools prints a paid price on the pages we opened, so cost is a sales conversation. What differs is the way in. Some offer a free sign-up or a limited free tier, some a demo, and some only a contact form. Free access is a quick way to test whether the data answers your question before you pay. Ask about seat limits, data export rights and how long history goes back.

market_notes: The ten services divide by platform. Sensor Tower, AppMagic, Appfigures, Apptopia and Game Refinery lean on mobile data; Gamalytic, VGInsights and SteamSpy focus on Steam; GameDiscoverCo spans Steam and console; Niko Partners sells regional research for Asia and MENA. Three offer a free way in on the pages we read: Sensor Tower with a free sign-up, Appfigures with a free start, and Game Refinery with free access. No vendor among the ten prints a paid price on the pages we opened.

The trade-off is breadth against trust. Broad platforms such as Sensor Tower cover many industries and use panel and store API data, while narrow ones like SteamSpy state their limits openly: its own About page warns that it is often wrong by some margin and that small games have very unreliable numbers. VGInsights is hosted under Sensor Tower, so those two are related. Customer counts and coverage figures, such as GameDiscoverCo's 110 teams or Gamalytic's 100,000+ Steam games, are vendor claims we could not verify.

how_to_choose.title: Name the question before you pick a tool
how_to_choose.text: Write the decision in one sentence: size a mobile genre, price a Steam release, time a launch around live events, or plan a regional entry in Southeast Asia. Then match it. Revenue by genre on mobile points to AppMagic or Sensor Tower, Steam sales comparables to Gamalytic or VGInsights, and regional research to Niko Partners. Starting from the question keeps you from buying a subscription for data you will open once.

how_to_choose.title: Use free access and demos to test accuracy
how_to_choose.text: Pick three games you know well, ideally ones where you have seen real numbers from a friend or a postmortem, and look them up in each shortlisted tool. Compare the output with what you know. A service that gets the order of magnitude right and states its error is useful; one that is far off, or does not list the game, is not. Free sign-ups from Sensor Tower, Appfigures and Game Refinery make this cheap.

how_to_choose.title: Plan for sources to disagree
how_to_choose.text: Do not treat one tool as ground truth. Estimates for the same game differ between vendors because each samples different panels and models different conversion factors. Use two sources for any number that drives a budget, and write the range, not a point figure, in your business plan. When you ask for a quote, ask how far back data goes and whether exports are allowed, since re-building a chart later may need a new license.

faqs.q: What is the best game market intelligence tool in 2026?
faqs.a: Sensor Tower is the broadest pick: a platform covering mobile apps, advertising, web and gaming, with GameIQ for games and a free sign-up. GameDiscoverCo is better for Steam and console wishlists, sales forecasts and MCP access, and AppMagic is better for mobile genre and publisher comparison.

faqs.q: How accurate are Steam revenue estimates from these tools?
faqs.a: They are models, not reports. SteamSpy's About page says its owner numbers carry a margin of error at 98% confidence and that stats for small games are very unreliable. Treat any figure for a small game as a range, compare at least two sources, and expect larger errors for games with few owners.

faqs.q: Is there a free game market intelligence tool?
faqs.a: Partly. Sensor Tower offers a free sign-up and a free Chrome extension called Web Insights, Appfigures shows a Get Started Free button with no credit card required, and Game Refinery's homepage offers access for free. SteamSpy and Niko Partners also publish free pages or bulletins, though full data is paid or limited.

faqs.q: Which tool shows wishlists for Steam games?
faqs.a: GameDiscoverCo lists wishlists among its data on Steam sales, revenue and audiences, plus Next Fest rankings and sales forecasts from comparable games. Access to its data comes through a Pro plan, and the homepage offers a demo rather than prices.

faqs.q: Do I need market intelligence if I am a solo indie developer?
faqs.a: You may not need a paid subscription. A solo developer can start with a Sensor Tower free sign-up, a Game Refinery free access request or a look at the SteamSpy pages before paying for anything. Paid tools become worthwhile when a publisher pitch, investor deck or a budget decision depends on comparable-game revenue.

faqs.q: What does Apptopia sell and who is it for?
faqs.a: Apptopia sells mobile app performance and consumer activity data, including downloads, in-app purchase revenue, DAU and MAU, retention and SDK installs. Its pages are written for investors, brands and sales teams, with a base package described as enterprise-level and pricing on quote.

faqs.q: Which tool covers games in Asia and the Middle East?
faqs.a: Niko Partners focuses on video games and esports in Asia and MENA, selling reports, data trackers, a NikoIQ knowledge base and custom consulting. Its homepage lists a livestreaming tracker and publishes free bulletins and white papers. Prices are not shown.

tools.name: Sensor Tower
tools.tagline: Digital market insights platform with a gaming product
tools.best_for: Studios wanting mobile and ad data together
tools.pricing: Paid prices are not listed; the home page has a Sign Up for Free button and a free Chrome extension, Web Insights, plus Request Demo and Contact Sales options.
tools.platforms: Mobile apps, web, advertising channels, retail media, gaming and audiences
tools.summary: First because it covers the widest range of data, from app performance to ad spend, includes a gaming product and offers a free start.
tools.verdict: Sensor Tower describes itself as a digital market insights platform covering mobile apps, advertising and audiences, and its home page lists App Performance Insights, Pathmatics, Web Insights and Gaming Insights (GameIQ) as product areas. The data comes from a global panel of consumers and app store APIs, according to the page. It names Activision Blizzard, Duolingo, Spotify and Coca-Cola among its users. A free sign-up lets a studio test coverage first, which is unusual in this field. For a mid-size mobile studio it is the most complete single source.
tools.weaknesses: Paid prices are not listed, and the breadth means a studio that needs only Steam data pays for a platform much larger than its question. The list of customers and cited outlets is vendor-reported.
tools.wrong_for: Steam-only indies should look at Gamalytic or VGInsights. Studios needing regional research for Asia should consider Niko Partners.

tools.name: GameDiscoverCo
tools.tagline: Steam and console data on sales, wishlists and audiences
tools.best_for: PC and console teams planning a launch
tools.pricing: No prices on the home page; features are sold under GameDiscoverCo Pro, and the page offers Book a demo and Ask about access.
tools.platforms: Steam, PlayStation, Xbox and Switch data; MCP and API access
tools.summary: Second because wishlist data, console coverage and forecasts from comparable games speak directly to a PC or console launch plan.
tools.verdict: GameDiscoverCo offers Steam, console and MCP or API data for games-industry analysis, and its home page lists sales, revenue, wishlists and audience figures, sales forecasts built from comparable games and Next Fest rankings. Coverage reaches PlayStation, Xbox and Switch as well as Steam, which is rare in this field. The MCP and API access, which the page says requires its Pro plan, lets analysts query the data through assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude. The page says it is trusted by over 110 teams, naming Bandai Namco, Krafton, Team17 and Raw Fury.
tools.weaknesses: No prices are shown, and MCP access depends on a Pro plan with access enabled, so the cheapest route in is unclear. Mobile data is not part of the pitch, and the customer count is a vendor claim.
tools.wrong_for: Mobile studios should start with Sensor Tower or AppMagic. Developers who only need free Steam lookups can try SteamSpy.

tools.name: AppMagic
tools.tagline: Mobile app market intelligence with genre classification
tools.best_for: Mobile teams researching genres and publishers
tools.pricing: The pricing page lets you build your own feature set from dashboards, tools and data access; prices are not in the fetched text.
tools.platforms: Mobile apps (iOS and Android market data)
tools.summary: Third because genre classification, publisher comparison and soft launch detection target mobile game research, though prices stay hidden.
tools.verdict: AppMagic describes itself as a service for mobile app market intelligence designed for market research. Its meta description highlights high-precision classification of app genres, comparison of multiple apps and publishers, and detection of successful soft launches. The pricing page lets a buyer assemble a plan from dashboards, tools and data access instead of picking a fixed tier, which suits a studio that needs only revenue estimates and not a full suite. Soft launch detection is useful for spotting a competitor's test market early.
tools.weaknesses: The home page is rendered by JavaScript, so we took facts from its meta description; prices are not visible and the company is not named in the text we read. Console and Steam data are not mentioned.
tools.wrong_for: Steam and console teams should look at GameDiscoverCo or Gamalytic. Those who want a free entry point should try Sensor Tower's sign-up.

tools.name: VGInsights
tools.tagline: Video Game Insights database with 50+ datapoints per game
tools.pricing: Pricing is not shown in the fetched text; the product has a pricing page hosted on app.sensortower.com.
tools.summary: Fourth because 50+ datapoints for over 150,000 games give depth for comparables, while the product now lives inside Sensor Tower.
tools.verdict: Video Game Insights, shortened to VGI, is a games industry data product for developers, publishers and anyone interested in video game market research. It provides 50+ datapoints per game for over 150,000 games, which makes it a deep source for building comparable-game lists. The vginsights.com domain redirects to Sensor Tower's VGI product page, so the product now sits under the same company as the first-ranked tool. For a PC-focused team that wants per-title depth over a broad dashboard, it is a direct route to that data.
tools.weaknesses: The vendor page is rendered by JavaScript and we could read only the meta description; prices and platform coverage are not visible. Because it is hosted by Sensor Tower, it is not an independent second opinion against that vendor.
tools.wrong_for: Mobile-only teams should use Sensor Tower or AppMagic directly. Those wanting an explicitly independent source for cross-checking should add Gamalytic.

tools.name: Gamalytic
tools.tagline: Database of 100,000+ Steam games with estimated sales
tools.pricing: A Pricing link appears in the navigation, but no plan details or prices are on the home page; the pricing page was not opened.
tools.summary: Fifth because it is a focused Steam database with revenue, sales and player estimates, but its pages show no prices or method notes.
tools.verdict: Gamalytic describes itself as a database of 100,000+ Steam games with estimated revenue, sales and player data, built for game developers, market researchers and game enthusiasts. Lists of games, publishers, genres and tags let a developer pull up comparables for a pitch or launch plan without an enterprise contract. The home page states that it is not affiliated with Valve or Steam in any way, which is worth knowing when judging the data's origin. For an indie team sizing a Steam release, it is a direct and narrow tool.
tools.weaknesses: The home page does not show prices, free access or how the estimates are produced, and the pricing page was not opened. It covers Steam only, with no mobile or console view.
tools.wrong_for: Mobile or console teams should look at AppMagic or GameDiscoverCo. Teams that need documented error margins should read SteamSpy's notes alongside it.

tools.name: Game Refinery
tools.tagline: Mobile game dataset and live events tracker
tools.pricing: The homepage offers Access for free and a Contact us or schedule a trial option; no paid prices are shown on the opened pages.
tools.platforms: Mobile games; live events data across all platforms per the homepage
tools.summary: Sixth because live events, mechanics and player motivation data suit live-ops planning, though it covers mobile and shows no paid prices.
tools.verdict: GameRefinery describes itself as the market's most comprehensive dataset for mobile games, covering live events, gameplay mechanics, player motivations and monetization strategies. The Live Events Tracker answers a question revenue tools cannot: what a competitor ran last month and when. The footer identifies the company as part of Liftoff, and a newer AppRefinery product is listed on the homepage. Free access is offered, with a contact route for a trial, so a live-ops lead can test the tracker before paying.
tools.weaknesses: It is mobile-centered, no paid prices are shown, and what the free access includes is not described. Its comprehensive claim is vendor-made.
tools.wrong_for: Steam or console teams should choose Gamalytic or GameDiscoverCo. Revenue-focused users who want store ranking estimates should see AppMagic.

tools.name: Appfigures
tools.tagline: App downloads, revenue, rankings, reviews and keywords tracker
tools.pricing: No pricing tiers on the home page; it shows a Get Started Free button and says no credit card required.
tools.platforms: Live App Store and Google Play data
tools.summary: Seventh because it mixes competitor figures with your own store analytics and reviews, but is general to apps rather than games.
tools.verdict: Appfigures describes itself as a platform for tracking app downloads, revenue and market trends, researching competitors and finding keywords. For a studio it works as a dashboard that joins competitor estimates with the studio's own store analytics, review monitoring and keyword tracking. The home page shows live App Store and Google Play data and says it tracks SDK additions and removals for SDK makers. A Get Started Free button with no credit card gives a cheap trial. That mix suits a small mobile studio.
tools.weaknesses: Plan limits and tiers are not described on the home page, so it is unclear what the free start includes. The 28M apps and 11B downloads figures are self-reported and unverified, and nothing is specific to games.
tools.wrong_for: Teams researching genres, events and mechanics should pick Game Refinery or AppMagic. Steam developers get nothing from it.

tools.name: Apptopia
tools.tagline: Mobile app performance data aimed at investors and brands
tools.pricing: Custom pricing; the investor pricing page says the base package is an enterprise-level service, with flexible plans for brands and for MSP and sales teams.
tools.summary: Eighth because the metrics are deep, including DAU, retention and churn, but the product is aimed at investors and enterprise buyers.
tools.verdict: Apptopia provides mobile app consumer activity data, and its home page says it is trusted by more than 200 leading firms. Metrics include downloads, in-app purchase revenue, DAU and MAU, retention by cohort, churn and SDK installs and uninstalls. The investor pricing page says its Base dataset covers 3,500+ tickers with point-in-time mapping across 160+ countries and 10 years of history. A publisher doing due diligence on a listed mobile company will see the value; a small studio will mostly find it too large for its question.
tools.weaknesses: Its pages are written for investors, brands and sales teams, not game developers, and the base package is described as enterprise-level with custom pricing. Games are not singled out in the text we read.
tools.wrong_for: Small developers should try Appfigures or Sensor Tower's free sign-up. Genre and live-event research belongs with Game Refinery.

tools.name: Niko Partners
tools.tagline: Research on video games and esports in Asia and MENA
tools.best_for: Publishers planning Asia or MENA entry
tools.pricing: Not stated on the opened page; the page offers a NikoIQ demo and contact options.
tools.platforms: Web knowledge base (NikoIQ), reports and data trackers
tools.summary: Ninth because it is the only regional research firm here, strong for Asia and MENA but irrelevant to a purely Western launch.
tools.verdict: Niko Partners describes itself as delivering market data and insights for video games and esports in Asia and MENA. Its products are NikoIQ, an interactive knowledge base, data and insights trackers, research reports and custom consulting, plus a livestreaming tracker mentioned in its latest insights. The homepage lists free bulletins and white papers, which gives an entry point without a contract, and quotes executives at Zynga, NCSOFT and Savvy Games Group. A publisher planning to localize and sell in Southeast Asia or the Middle East gets regional depth that global dashboards lack.
tools.weaknesses: Coverage is limited to Asia and MENA, no prices are shown, and the product is research and consulting rather than a self-serve dataset. Testimonials on the page are vendor-selected.
tools.wrong_for: Teams launching in Western markets should choose Sensor Tower or GameDiscoverCo. Solo developers needing a cheap lookup should use SteamSpy.

tools.name: SteamSpy
tools.tagline: Owner estimates for Steam games from public profile data
tools.best_for: Quick rough checks on Steam titles
tools.pricing: No prices appear on the opened pages; the About page calls it a side project of its author.
features: Owner estimates with margin of error
tools.summary: Tenth because its own notes say it is often wrong and still in beta, with a copyright line that ends in 2021.
tools.verdict: SteamSpy says it gathers data from Steam user profiles to present game statistics for indie developers, journalists, students and PC gaming fans. Its pages list genres, tags, companies and countries, and each game shows an owners figure with a stated margin of error. The About page is candid: it explains the 98% confidence margin, warns that stats for games with small samples are very unreliable and that free weekends distort owner counts. That honesty makes it a fair first look, not a basis for a budget.
tools.weaknesses: The About page says the site is still in beta and often wrong, owners do not equal sales, and the copyright range is 2015-2021, so freshness is a concern. It is a side project of one author with no stated pricing or support.
tools.wrong_for: Anyone needing dependable revenue figures should look at Gamalytic, VGInsights or GameDiscoverCo. Mobile teams get nothing from it.
